title: Figure 3. Enlarged rings turn more slowly and respond less to weak boundary input
role: Separates strong-cue turning from linear boundary susceptibility and tests the cytosolic conduction mechanism.
legend: Fast cytosol removes Wave-pinning’s size-dependent boundary gain; an isolated-front prediction gives its absolute native-ring gains within 6.9–8.0% without fitting them. Native gain declines less in Holmes and Spring. Goryachev’s gain falls strongly, but no conduction-law comparison is made for that model.

A, Native Wave-pinning C30 active-concentration kymographs for a cue overlapping the incumbent’s 10%-contrast contour (edge gap −1) or separated from it (gap 4). Time starts at cue onset; cyan bars show spatial cue support. White dashed lines mark withdrawal after 95% of the target heading change; subsequent single-domain relaxation is included. Native cue peak 0.1 and support 3 are unchanged.

B, Time to turn halfway toward a continuous cue against its edge gap, at C30, 37.8 and 47.6 (Spring resting sizes 2.5, 3.15 and 3.97). Shades denote size within each model. Open triangles with upward arrows are right-censored lower bounds; grey spans mark gaps at which heading was undefined at one or more sizes. These strong-cue turning times are distinct from weak-pulse susceptibility.

C, Susceptibility to a weak Gaussian pulse, permanent displacement per peak×duration dose, against position at C40 (Spring resting size 2). Colored lines use the native translation-mode adjoint at f=0.001 (Spring mean input 0.004); grey curves and right axes show the same stationary mean active profile. The Gaussian SD is 1.5 (Spring 0.15). Signed gain is localized to the two lateral boundaries.

D, Wave-pinning shared permanent boundary displacement against edge-pulse peak divided by reference input 0.1, at C20 and C60; duration 50. Dashed lines use the weak-input gain. Ten-percent departures are bracketed between 5–20% of reference input in Wave-pinning, 2.6–5% in Holmes, 1.3–2.6% in Spring and 2.6–20% in Goryachev (neighboring tested amplitudes, pooled size ranges). Dose-matched duration sweeps agree within 0.2%.

E, Native edge gain normalized to each model’s smallest size, against relative resting size. Wave-pinning’s solid curve is predicted from the isolated front: G=(λ/2)/(1+C/C*), C*=76.3, with stationary domain fraction θ and no fitted ring gains. Holmes’s dashed curve is fitted to native inverse gain, 1/G=a+bC, C*=a/b≈403. Spring’s dashed conduction curve uses C*≈49, fitted to the free-conduction penalty G(1000,C)/G(D,C)−1 against C/D for D≥1; the dash-dot curve multiplies that fit by the measured free-conduction gain rise. This empirical correction and the apparent native crossover (about 140) are distinct from an isolated-front prediction. Goryachev has points only. Spring’s actual circumference includes extension; its native points use mean input 0.004, the sweep 0.0004. Fit-definition sensitivity is reported in the readme.

F, Wave-pinning adjoint edge gain against circumference at inactive diffusivities 2.5, 5, 10 (native), 20, 40, 100 and 1000. Every point uses the same weak mean input and unchanged reaction kinetics. All 35 Wave-pinning preparations retain a polarized branch, including Dᵥ=2.5 at C60 where the pilot reported domain loss. Fast cytosol largely removes the native size dependence. All quantities use model-native units; none is a calibrated migration velocity or biochemical dose.
narrative: Larger rings take longer to turn toward a continuous cue across the tested positions. Overlap distinguishes incumbent sliding from nucleation and replacement by a separate domain; further separation has relatively little effect outside Goryachev. These strong-cue responses are distinct from weak-pulse gain.
Weak-input translation susceptibility is localized to the two lateral boundaries. Native gain falls substantially with size in Wave-pinning and Goryachev, and changes little in Holmes and Spring.

Fast cytosol removes Wave-pinning’s size dependence: the C60/C20 gain ratio rises from about 0.70 at native diffusivity to 1.00 at fast diffusivity, with unchanged reaction kinetics. This perturbation identifies a cytosolic-transport contribution to boundary gain.

An isolated-front conduction law predicts absolute native Wave-pinning gains within 6.9–8.0% without fitting ring gains. Holmes is represented by a native inverse-gain fit. Spring’s fitted transport factor is offset by an independently measured free-conduction gain rise, so its corrected curve is empirical and the simple C/D law does not collapse all Spring data.
measurements: At matched cue dose and boundary offset in a WGD+/− pair, vary photoactivation from straddling to separated relative to the incumbent boundary and measure half-turn time, incumbent sliding and challenger replacement. The models predict longer WGD+ half-turn times; Goryachev lacks the same overlap-to-separation regime switch. This strong-cue assay is distinct from the linear response.

Apply a weak brief pulse at one lateral boundary and measure permanent common displacement of both edges. At matched dose, WGD+ displacement is predicted to decrease strongly for Wave-pinning- and Goryachev-like susceptibility classes, but little for Holmes- and Spring-like classes. This contrast alone cannot separate conduction from pool depletion; combine it with inactive-pool mobility and Figure 2 first-rise measurements.

Compare spontaneous lateral-edge and plateau input/activity fluctuations in WGD− and WGD+. Edge fluctuations should dominate weak heading drift. Under shared input statistics, response shape and correlated edge motion, the squared gain ratio predicts physical drift ratio; angular drift additionally includes the squared inverse perimeter ratio (Eq. 3.2). This conditional drift prediction does not establish the Goryachev jump mechanism or a migration-velocity law.
limitations: Strong turning and weak response use different amplitudes and size grids; susceptibility does not explain the strong turning times.
Spring’s low-diffusivity branch changes lie outside the reported conduction law. Goryachev has no fitted conduction curve.
Model time, input and size have no cross-model biological calibration.

equations.description: Wave-pinning crossover uses the isolated front and stationary domain fraction; Holmes uses the native inverse-gain regression and Spring uses the diffusivity-penalty regression, with intrinsic free-conduction rise shown explicitly.
Conditional prediction for shared input statistics, response shape and correlated edge motion. The first ratio is physical boundary drift; angular decorrelation additionally includes geometry.
